title: Propranolol and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on a Beta Blocker?
excerpt: Can you drink on propranolol? How the beta blocker and alcohol interact, what it means for a 10 mg dose before a wedding or speech, daily use, and warning signs that need a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on propranolol? How it interacts with alcohol, what to know about a 10 mg dose before a wedding or speech, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** propranolol and alcohol both lower your blood pressure, and together they can drop it far enough to make you dizzy, lightheaded, or faint, particularly when you stand up quickly. Alcohol can also change how much propranolol reaches your bloodstream, and propranolol can hide the warning signs of low blood sugar that drinking on an empty stomach can cause. For many healthy adults, a drink or two while taking a low dose (like 10 mg before a speech) is something doctors often allow with care. Heavier drinking on propranolol is where the real risk sits.

**The quick rules:** Don't stop a daily propranolol prescription so you can drink. Test any new dose on a quiet day before mixing it with alcohol. Eat first, keep to one or two drinks, alternate with water, and stand up slowly. Stop drinking if you feel dizzy, faint, unusually tired, or your heartbeat feels very slow.

> **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist.** This article explains general research and prescribing guidance. It is not medical advice and doesn't replace someone who knows your health history and your full medication list. **Ask before drinking on propranolol if** you take it for a heart condition, high blood pressure, liver disease, or migraines; you have diabetes or asthma; you take other blood pressure, heart, anxiety, or sleep medicines; or you're over 65. **Get emergency care (911 in the US) for** fainting, chest pain, a very slow or irregular pulse, severe breathlessness or wheezing, or confusion.

## How Propranolol and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Propranolol (brand names include Inderal, Inderal LA, and InnoPran XL) is a **beta blocker**. It works by blocking the effects of adrenaline on your body. Adrenaline speeds up the heart, makes it pump harder, makes your hands shake, and drives that pounding, sweaty feeling you get before something stressful. Propranolol takes the edge off all of that.

It's a "non-selective" beta blocker, meaning it blocks two types of adrenaline receptor: the beta-1 receptors mostly in the heart, and the beta-2 receptors in the airways, blood vessels, and muscles. It also crosses into the brain more easily than many other beta blockers. That combination is why it's used for such a wide range of things: high blood pressure, angina, irregular heart rhythms, migraine prevention, essential tremor, overactive thyroid symptoms, and, off-label, performance anxiety.

Alcohol meets propranolol in three main places.

### 1. Blood pressure: two drops added together

Alcohol widens (dilates) blood vessels in the hours after you drink. That's why your face can flush and why you can feel lightheaded getting up from the table after a few drinks. Propranolol lowers blood pressure by slowing the heart and reducing how hard it pumps. Normally, when your blood pressure dips, your body reacts by speeding up your heart to compensate. Propranolol blocks that reflex.

Put them together and you get a bigger drop in blood pressure, with less of the automatic correction your body would normally make. The most common result is **orthostatic hypotension**, a fancy name for feeling dizzy or blacking out briefly when you go from sitting to standing. That's why the most common complaint from people who mix the two is lightheadedness, and the main danger is a fall.

### 2. Blood levels: alcohol can change how much drug you get

Propranolol is heavily processed by the liver. Only a fraction of each swallowed dose makes it into circulation, because the liver breaks a large share of it down on the first pass. Alcohol uses some of the same liver machinery, and it also affects how fast your stomach empties and how much blood flows through the liver.

The US prescribing information for propranolol lists alcohol as an interaction and notes it may raise propranolol levels in the blood. Research over the years has found alcohol can shift propranolol levels, and the size and direction of the effect hasn't been consistent from study to study. The practical takeaway is simple: you can't predict exactly how strong your dose will feel on a night you're drinking, which is one more reason to keep the amount modest.

### 3. Masked warning signs

A racing heart and trembling hands are your body's alarm bells for several problems, including low blood sugar. Drinking, especially without food, can push blood sugar down, and the effect can show up hours later, sometimes overnight. Propranolol blunts those alarm bells. Sweating usually still happens, but the shakiness and pounding heart that would normally tip you off may not appear.

For most healthy people this is a minor concern. For anyone with diabetes, particularly people who use insulin or medicines that lower blood sugar, it matters a lot. It's one of the reasons propranolol labels carry a warning for people with diabetes.

### What propranolol doesn't do

Propranolol does not make you less drunk, and it doesn't speed up how quickly your body clears alcohol. Because it can make you feel calmer, it may make you *feel* more in control than you actually are. Your coordination, judgment, and reaction time are just as affected as they'd be without it, and possibly more if your blood pressure is low.

## What Official Guidance Says

Propranolol labels and pharmacy leaflets don't usually say "never drink." The general message from prescribing information, the UK's NHS medicine pages, and pharmacist references runs along the same lines:

- Alcohol can add to the blood-pressure-lowering effect and make you feel dizzy or lightheaded.
- It's sensible to avoid or limit alcohol, at least until you know how propranolol affects you.
- Don't stop propranolol suddenly without talking to your doctor.

In other words, the advice is to be cautious and check, not a flat ban. Your own doctor may be stricter if you take propranolol for a heart condition, have liver disease, or drink regularly.

## Propranolol 10 mg Before a Wedding or Speech: Can You Still Drink?

This is the situation most people searching this topic are in. You've been prescribed a small as-needed dose of propranolol, often 10 mg to 40 mg, to take before a best-man speech, a presentation, an exam, or walking down the aisle. Then there's a champagne toast, an open bar, and a long evening.

Here's how to think about it.

**The dose matters.** A single 10 mg dose is low. Many healthy adults who take it for performance anxiety notice little besides a calmer heartbeat and steadier hands. Higher as-needed doses lower blood pressure and heart rate more, which leaves less room before alcohol makes you lightheaded.

**The timing matters.** Regular (immediate-release) propranolol usually reaches its peak within about one to two hours, which is why it's typically taken roughly an hour before the event. Its effect on heart rate fades over several hours. If you took 10 mg before a 2 p.m. ceremony and your first drink is a toast at 7 p.m., the overlap is much smaller than if you took it at 6:30 and started drinking at 7.

**A few practical steps help a lot:**

1. **Do a test run.** Take your prescribed dose on an ordinary day, with no alcohol, before the big event. That way you know how it feels on its own, and you won't be finding out for the first time in a suit or dress in a hot room. Many prescribers recommend this anyway.
2. **Eat a real meal before you drink.** Food slows alcohol absorption and helps keep your blood sugar steady.
3. **Keep it to one or two drinks, and pace them.** Alternate each drink with a glass of water.
4. **Watch out for heat and standing still.** Long ceremonies, crowded rooms, hot weather, and standing in a receiving line all pool blood in your legs. Add alcohol and a beta blocker, and fainting gets more likely. Shift your weight, flex your calves, and sit down if you feel off.
5. **Take care on the dance floor.** Propranolol limits how high your heart rate can climb, so you may tire faster and feel breathless sooner during hard exercise.
6. **Stand up slowly.** Especially after sitting through dinner.

If you feel dizzy, foggy, or like you might faint, stop drinking, sit or lie down with your legs raised, and drink water. If you actually faint, have chest pain, or don't recover quickly, get medical help.

**Don't share your propranolol.** It's common at weddings for someone to hand a nervous friend a pill. Propranolol is unsafe for people with asthma, certain heart rhythm problems, very slow heart rates, and some other conditions. It's a prescription medicine for a reason.

## Daily Propranolol for Blood Pressure, Heart, or Migraines

If you take propranolol every day, the picture is different, because there's no "gap" in which the drug is out of your system. The question isn't when you can drink but how much.

**Never skip doses to drink.** Stopping a beta blocker suddenly can cause a rebound: a fast heart rate, palpitations, a spike in blood pressure, and in people with heart disease, worsening chest pain or even a heart attack. The prescribing information carries a strong warning about abrupt withdrawal. If you're worried about mixing, the right move is to drink less, not to stop the medicine.

**Regular drinking works against the reason you're on it.** Heavy or regular drinking raises blood pressure over time, can trigger irregular heart rhythms, and is a common migraine trigger. If you take propranolol for any of those, alcohol is pulling in the opposite direction. Our guide to [alcohol and blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) explains why even moderate regular drinking tends to push readings up.

**Liver disease changes everything.** Propranolol is sometimes prescribed for people with cirrhosis to reduce pressure in the veins around the liver. In that situation, any alcohol is usually off the table, and the decision belongs entirely to your liver specialist.

**Extended-release capsules.** Long-acting forms like Inderal LA and InnoPran XL release the drug over the day. Your pharmacist can tell you whether there's any specific advice for your formulation; with long-acting capsules, you should swallow them whole and never open or crush them.

## Side Effects That Alcohol Can Make Worse

Propranolol's common side effects overlap with how alcohol makes you feel. Drinking can stack on top of them.

| Effect | From propranolol | What alcohol adds |
|---|---|---|
| Dizziness, lightheadedness | Lower blood pressure and heart rate | Widened blood vessels, dehydration |
| Tiredness, low energy | A common side effect, especially early on | Sedation, poor-quality sleep |
| Cold hands and feet | Reduced blood flow to the skin | Heat loss through flushed skin later on |
| Vivid dreams, broken sleep | Reported by some users | Alcohol fragments the second half of the night |
| Low mood | Reported occasionally | Alcohol is a depressant, and next-day mood dips are common |
| Masked low blood sugar | Hides tremor and racing heart | Drinking without food can lower blood sugar |

If any of these show up after only a drink or two, take it as a sign that your personal limit on propranolol is lower than you'd expect, and mention it to your doctor.

## Propranolol, Hangovers, and Hangxiety

Some people search this because they wake up after drinking with a pounding heart and a wave of dread, often called "hangxiety," and wonder whether propranolol would help.

Propranolol can calm the physical side of anxiety, such as a racing pulse and shaky hands. That's why it's used for performance nerves. But a hangover is more than adrenaline. It involves dehydration, poor sleep, irritation of the stomach, inflammation, and the after-effects of alcohol on brain chemistry. Propranolol touches none of those. It also lowers blood pressure, and if you're dehydrated and lightheaded the morning after, that can make things worse.

If propranolol has been prescribed to you for anxiety, ask your doctor whether using it the morning after drinking is reasonable for you. Don't take someone else's, and don't start taking it regularly to cope with hangovers. If a racing heart after drinking is a regular pattern for you, our guide to [a racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) covers the common causes and when it's worth getting checked. For the anxiety side, see our [complete guide to hangxiety](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research).

## Can Propranolol Hide Alcohol Withdrawal?

This is worth knowing even if it doesn't apply to you. Beta blockers are occasionally used in hospital alongside other treatment for alcohol withdrawal, because they calm the racing heart and tremor. That same effect means propranolol can hide early withdrawal signs.

If you've been drinking heavily every day for a while and you stop or cut down sharply, the usual warning signs are shaking, sweating, a racing heart, anxiety, nausea, and trouble sleeping, typically starting within a day or so. On propranolol you might not get the shaking or the fast heartbeat, but the underlying problem is still there. Severe withdrawal can cause seizures or confusion and needs medical care. If you drink daily and plan to stop, talk to a doctor first. If you notice confusion, seeing or hearing things that aren't there, or a seizure, call 911.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Talk to your doctor before drinking at all on propranolol if any of these apply:

- **You have diabetes**, especially if you use insulin or a sulfonylurea. Propranolol masks low-blood-sugar warning signs, and alcohol can cause low blood sugar.
- **You have asthma or COPD.** Propranolol can tighten the airways, and some alcoholic drinks (for example, those high in sulfites) trigger asthma in sensitive people.
- **You have a heart condition** such as heart failure, angina, or a slow heart rhythm.
- **You have liver disease**, including cirrhosis.
- **You're over 65.** Blood pressure drops and falls are more common and more serious with age.
- **You take other medicines that lower blood pressure or cause drowsiness**, such as other blood pressure pills, nitrates, erectile dysfunction medicines, benzodiazepines, sleep aids, opioids, or some antidepressants. Each can add to the effect.
- **You take medicines that change propranolol levels.** Some antidepressants and other drugs alter how the liver handles propranolol. Your pharmacist can check your list in a minute.

For a broader look at how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## When to Get Help

**Call 911 or go to the emergency department if you or someone else has:**

- Fainting, especially with a fall or head injury
- Chest pain or pressure
- A very slow pulse (well below your normal) with dizziness or weakness
- Wheezing or trouble breathing
- Confusion, extreme drowsiness, or being hard to wake
- Signs of low blood sugar that don't improve with food or sugar: sweating, confusion, unusual behavior

**Call your doctor or pharmacist soon if you notice:**

- Lightheadedness every time you drink, even with small amounts
- Swollen ankles or new shortness of breath
- Low mood that's getting worse
- You've accidentally taken extra propranolol

If you think someone has taken too much propranolol, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) right away. A beta blocker overdose can be serious and is much more dangerous combined with alcohol.

## Practical Checklist Before You Drink on Propranolol

1. Know your dose and formulation (as-needed immediate-release, daily tablets, or long-acting capsules).
2. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist once: "Is it OK for me to have a drink or two on this?"
3. Try the medicine alone before combining it with alcohol.
4. Eat first. Pace yourself. Alternate with water.
5. Stand up slowly and sit down at the first sign of dizziness.
6. Don't drive. The combination can affect alertness and blood pressure, and the legal limit doesn't account for medication.
7. Never skip or stop a daily dose to make room for drinking.

## Where Supplements Fit (and Where They Don't)

No supplement makes propranolol and alcohol a safe combination, and none should replace the steps above. The most useful thing you can do is drink less on the nights you take it. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence: eating, pacing, water, and sleep.

Some people use **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, on nights out. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. There are no published studies on DHM combined with propranolol, and there is no good evidence that DHM lessens the blood-pressure interaction. If you take propranolol daily, check with your pharmacist before adding any supplement. If you're cleared to try it, well-reviewed options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

Propranolol and alcohol both lower blood pressure, and propranolol stops your heart from speeding up to compensate. That's why the classic problem is dizziness or fainting, especially on standing. Alcohol can also shift propranolol levels unpredictably, and propranolol can hide the warning signs of low blood sugar.

For a one-off low dose before a speech or wedding, a drink or two later on is often fine for healthy adults, as long as you've tested the dose first, eaten, paced yourself, and stayed alert for dizziness. If you take propranolol every day, never stop it to drink; keep alcohol light and ask your doctor what's right for your condition. And if anything feels seriously wrong, like fainting, chest pain, or trouble breathing, get help right away.

**Related reading:** [beta blockers and alcohol (all types)](/never-hungover/beta-blockers-and-alcohol).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking propranolol?**

Many people on propranolol can have a drink or two, but the combination can lower your blood pressure more than either one alone, which can make you dizzy, lightheaded, or faint, especially when you stand up. Alcohol can also change how much propranolol ends up in your blood. Ask your doctor or pharmacist what's sensible for you, and keep it light until you know how the two affect you together.

**Can I drink after taking 10 mg of propranolol for anxiety?**

A low as-needed dose like 10 mg before a speech or a wedding is the situation people ask about most. For many healthy adults, one or two drinks later in the day may be tolerated, but you are stacking two things that both lower blood pressure. Try the dose on a quiet day first, eat before you drink, go slowly, sit or stand up carefully, and stop if you feel dizzy. Check with the prescriber who gave you the propranolol, since they know your health history.

**How long after taking propranolol can I drink alcohol?**

There is no official waiting time. Regular (immediate-release) propranolol usually peaks within about 1 to 2 hours and its effect on heart rate wears off over several hours, while long-acting capsules work all day. Waiting until the dose has mostly worn off lowers the overlap, but if you take propranolol every day there is no gap, so the real question is how much you drink, not when. Your pharmacist can tell you how your specific form behaves.

**Should I skip my propranolol dose so I can drink?**

No, not if you take it daily. Stopping a beta blocker suddenly can cause a rebound fast heart rate, a jump in blood pressure, and in people with heart disease, chest pain or worse. If you take propranolol only as needed for performance anxiety, skipping it is simply your choice. For a daily prescription, keep taking it as directed and drink less instead, or ask your doctor before changing anything.

**Does propranolol hide the effects of alcohol?**

It can hide some warning signs. Propranolol blunts a racing heart and shakiness, which are the same signals your body uses to warn you about low blood sugar, and drinking without food can lower blood sugar. It may also make you feel calmer than you really are, so you can't use 'I don't feel shaky' as a guide to how much you've had. It does not make you less drunk.

**Can I take propranolol for a hangover or hangxiety?**

Only if it has been prescribed to you and your doctor is comfortable with that use. Propranolol may calm a pounding heart and shakiness, but it doesn't treat dehydration, poor sleep, or the other causes of a hangover, and taking it while still dehydrated can make lightheadedness worse. Never take someone else's propranolol: it is unsafe for people with asthma, some heart rhythm problems, and several other conditions.

**Is it dangerous to mix propranolol and alcohol?**

For most people taking a normal dose, a small amount of alcohol is unlikely to be dangerous, but the risk climbs with heavier drinking. The main problems are low blood pressure, fainting and falls, masked low blood sugar, and worse side effects like tiredness. Get emergency help for fainting with injury, chest pain, a very slow pulse, confusion, or trouble breathing.

**Is DHM safe to take with propranolol?**

There are no published studies on DHM together with propranolol, so nobody can say for sure. DHM is a supplement studied mainly in animals for its effects on alcohol and the liver, and there is no good evidence that it reduces the propranolol and alcohol interaction. If you take propranolol daily, ask your pharmacist before adding any supplement.
